Anishininew

Anishininew, also written Anisininew, identifies distinct peoples and communities in northeastern Manitoba and northwestern Ontario. Island Lake nations emphasize their own identity rather than the outside label Oji-Cree. Their histories connect family harvesting territories, treaty relationships, language education and contemporary institutions controlled by the communities themselves.

Names & relationshipsAnishininew/Anisininew is not an interchangeable label for Cree or Anishinaabe. Island Lake’s four nations are one regional grouping; community names and spellings in northern Ontario also need their own context.
An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
01

Names, identity and community scope

Wasagamack Anisininew Nation’s 2024 community guide explicitly rejects describing its people as part Cree and part Ojibwe. It recalls an Island Lake declaration in 2018 and a wider gathering of Anisininew nations in February 2024 affirming a distinct identity. The guide also explains that Oji-Cree can be offensive locally. Spellings vary across community publications; the names used by the particular nation should guide discussion. Island Lake is an important regional focus, rather than the full extent of Anishininew peoplehood.

Read the sources [1] Wasagamack Anisininew Nation / Teach For Canada [6] Kitchenuhmaykoosib Inninuwug

02

Island Lake homelands and treaty history

Garden Hill, Wasagamack, St. Theresa Point and Red Sucker Lake share an Island Lake history while maintaining separate communities. Wasagamack’s school history locates the community on Island Lake’s western shore and identifies its participation in the 1909 adhesion to Treaty 5. The community’s own guide dates that signing to August 13 at Old Post on Linklater Island and describes treaty promises as unfinished obligations. This local account makes land, education and harvesting central to the treaty relationship, rather than treating the signing as the end of Indigenous authority.

Read the sources [1] Wasagamack Anisininew Nation / Teach For Canada [2] Wasagamack First Nation School

03

Northern Ontario histories have their own institutions

Kitchenuhmaykoosib Inninuwug’s history describes Anishinewuk family groups managing customary hunting territories around Big Trout Lake, with headmen representing clans. Summer gatherings renewed relationships through ceremonies, teaching, feasts, exchange and trade. Its account dates the local Treaty 9 adhesion to July 5, 1929 and records an understanding that the people would retain control over customary lands and resources. Later settlements developed their own administrations. These histories show why a Manitoba regional council cannot stand in for every community identified by a related name.

Read the sources [6] Kitchenuhmaykoosib Inninuwug

04

Language and education in community hands

Garden Hill Anisininew Nation High School describes teaching through English while integrating Anisinimowin, the Island Lake dialect, and cultural learning. Elders and Knowledge Keepers contribute stories, teachings and perspectives alongside the provincial curriculum. Wasagamack First Nation School similarly describes traditional learning and Elder guidance as part of schooling under its own education authority. These are concrete institutions in which language and community knowledge remain part of young people’s education. Their distinct programs should not be reduced to a single generic account of northern Indigenous schooling.

Read the sources [2] Wasagamack First Nation School [3] Garden Hill Anisininew Nation High School

05

Health, food and collective self-determination

The four Island Lake First Nations created and govern Four Arrows Regional Health Authority. Its institutional history traces planning in 1999, formal authorization in 2000 and responsibility for regional health services in 2001. Its Kimeechiminan food program connects health with language, land, cultural teaching and food sharing. Projects described on the program’s site include gardening, harvesting, food skills and a Garden Hill food enterprise. This approach treats food sovereignty as community leadership over food systems and relationships, alongside access to nutritious groceries.
